title: Controlled Inputs — Text, Checkbox, Select, Textarea

subChunks.title: Controlled Inputs — Text, Checkbox, Select, Textarea
subChunks.hookHtml: In plain HTML, form inputs manage their own state — the browser owns what's in the box. In React, you take that ownership back. A controlled input is one where React state is the single source of truth: the value prop always reflects the current state, and every keystroke updates that state. This gives you complete control over form data at any moment — validation on every keystroke, derived values, conditional fields, and programmatic resets.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The controlled input pattern

An uncontrolled input has no value prop — the DOM owns its value. A controlled input always has a value prop tied to state and an onChange handler that updates that state:

// ❌ Uncontrolled — React doesn't know what's in the box
<input type="text" />

// ✅ Controlled — React owns the value
function SearchBox() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');

  return (
    <input
      type="text"
      value={query}
      onChange={e => setQuery(e.target.value)}
    />
  );
}

Text input

const [username, setUsername] = useState('');

<input
  type="text"
  value={username}
  onChange={e => setUsername(e.target.value)}
  placeholder="Enter username"
/>

Textarea

In HTML, <textarea> has its content as a child node. In React, it uses a value prop just like a text input:

const [bio, setBio] = useState('');

<textarea
  value={bio}
  onChange={e => setBio(e.target.value)}
  rows={4}
/>

Checkbox

Checkboxes use checked (boolean) instead of value, and read from e.target.checked:

const [agreed, setAgreed] = useState(false);

<input
  type="checkbox"
  checked={agreed}
  onChange={e => setAgreed(e.target.checked)}
/>
<label>I agree to the terms</label>

Select (dropdown)

Select uses value on the <select> element (not on the options):

const [tier, setTier] = useState('apprentice');

<select value={tier} onChange={e => setTier(e.target.value)}>
  <option value="apprentice">Apprentice</option>
  <option value="junior">Junior</option>
  <option value="senior">Senior</option>
  <option value="lead">Lead</option>
</select>

Handling multiple inputs with one handler

For forms with many fields, use the input's name attribute to route updates through one handler:

const [form, setForm] = useState({ username: '', email: '', tier: 'apprentice' });

function handleChange(e) {
  const { name, value, type, checked } = e.target;
  setForm(prev => ({
    ...prev,
    [name]: type === 'checkbox' ? checked : value,
  }));
}

<input name="username" value={form.username} onChange={handleChange} />
<input name="email" type="email" value={form.email} onChange={handleChange} />
<input name="agreed" type="checkbox" checked={form.agreed} onChange={handleChange} />

Vex: "React state is the single source of truth. The input doesn't hold any data — it just reflects what React already knows. This means you can read the entire form state at any moment, validate it, transform it, or reset it with a single setState call."

Programmatic reset

function handleReset() {
  setForm({ username: '', email: '', tier: 'apprentice' });
  // All inputs instantly clear — because they're controlled
}

storyBeats.text: Vex holds two identical-looking inkwells. 'One fills itself,' she says. 'The other only fills when I pour. The first is an uncontrolled input. The second is controlled.' She pours ink into the controlled one, watching it reflect exactly what she added.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: When React owns the value, you can do anything with it — validate every character, transform it, sync it to another field, reset it instantly. The browser's DOM state is just a mirror of your React state. The DOM never leads; it only follows.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a ProfileForm component with three controlled inputs:

  • A text input bound to username state — data-testid="username-input"
  • A select bound to tier state with options: Apprentice, Junior, Senior — data-testid="tier-select"
  • A checkbox bound to newsletter boolean state — data-testid="newsletter-checkbox"
  • A <p data-testid="summary"> showing: "{username} | {tier} | newsletter: {yes/no}"
  • A Reset button that clears all fields to their initial values

guidedPracticeTests.label: Typing into username input updates summary
Checking newsletter shows yes in summary

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a <SignupForm> from scratch. Fields: email (text), password (password type), role (select: user/admin), acceptTerms (checkbox). All inputs are controlled. Show a live preview div that displays all current values. On submit (button click), log the form object to console and reset all fields.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain controlled vs uncontrolled inputs to a developer who is used to jQuery. Why does React require you to keep input values in state? What does 'React is the single source of truth' mean in the context of a form? Include why checkbox requires `checked` and `e.target.checked` rather than `value` and `e.target.value`.

questions.prompt: What makes an input 'controlled' in React?
options: The input has a `value` prop bound to state and an `onChange` handler that updates that state
The input is inside a `<form>` element with a submit handler
The input uses `defaultValue` to set its initial value
The input's value is read with `document.getElementById` in an event handler
questions.answer: The input has a `value` prop bound to state and an `onChange` handler that updates that state
questions.explanation: A controlled input always has its value dictated by React state via the `value` prop. Every keystroke fires onChange, which updates the state, which updates the value prop — a full loop. Without the onChange handler, the input becomes read-only (React controls the value but nothing updates the state). defaultValue sets the initial value once but doesn't control ongoing edits.

questions.prompt: For a controlled checkbox, which props and event handler properties are correct?
options: Checkboxes cannot be controlled — they always manage their own state
questions.explanation: Checkboxes represent a boolean, not a string. React exposes this through the `checked` prop (controlled state) and `e.target.checked` (the new boolean value in the event). `value` on a checkbox is a separate string attribute used when grouping checkboxes in HTML forms — it's not the checked/unchecked state.

questions.prompt: A form has 8 fields. What is the most maintainable approach for handling all their onChange events?
options: Keep form values in a single state object, use the input's `name` attribute, and route all changes through one handler using `[e.target.name]: e.target.value`
Create 8 separate useState calls and 8 separate onChange handlers
Use a ref for each field and read all values on submit only
Use the browser's built-in FormData API via a submit event
questions.answer: Keep form values in a single state object, use the input's `name` attribute, and route all changes through one handler using `[e.target.name]: e.target.value`
questions.explanation: A single state object with a single generic handler using computed property names (`[name]`) scales to any number of fields without duplication. Eight separate useState calls and handlers works but doesn't scale and creates repetitive code. Refs make the form uncontrolled. FormData is valid but makes live validation harder since values aren't in state.
